text: Commit thy works unto the LORD, and thy thoughts shall be established.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb teaches that human plans succeed only when submitted to the Lord's providence, not human ingenuity. The establishing power belongs to God alone; our part is committal, not control.

text: Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.
digest: {firstname}, God grounds Joshua's courage entirely in His covenant presence, not in Joshua's own strength or experience. Biblical courage is always derivative, drawn from the certainty that the Lord goes before and with His people.

text: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's contentment in this passage, verses just before this one, is the actual context: he can be content in plenty or want because Christ supplies strength for either. This is not a promise of achievement but of sufficiency through union with Christ.

text: For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end.
digest: {firstname}, this promise was given to exiles told to build houses and seek the peace of Babylon for seventy years first. God's good plans often unfold through, not around, seasons of discipline and waiting.

text: Fear thou not; for I am with thee: be not dismayed; for I am thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.
digest: {firstname}, the triple "I am" in this verse echoes God's covenant name and character, the same God who is not far off but present with His people. Fear is displaced here by the doctrine of God's nearness and sovereign strengthening, not by mere positive thinking.

text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
digest: {firstname}, calling the Lord "my shepherd" is a covenantal claim of belonging, not sentiment. Because He is shepherd, His sheep are kept, provided for, and led, so that lack itself becomes theologically impossible for those who are His.

text: And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
digest: {firstname}, Paul is instructing bondservants here, elevating even the lowest labor into an act done for Christ Himself. Work becomes worship when its ultimate audience is understood to be the Lord, not any human master.

text: And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
digest: {firstname}, Paul ties well-doing to an eschatological harvest, one that comes "in due season," a time appointed by God, not by our impatience. Perseverance in good works rests on the certainty of a future reckoning secured by God, not on visible results now.

text: Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
digest: {firstname}, trusting the Lord "with all thine heart" stands in deliberate contrast to leaning on one's own understanding, exposing how limited human reasoning is apart from revelation. Wisdom begins by displacing self-reliance with wholehearted trust in God's revealed will.

text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus places the kingdom of God and His righteousness as the supreme priority, promising that provision follows rightly ordered devotion. This is a call to right worship first, from which every other need is entrusted to the Father's care.

text: A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
digest: {firstname}, false balances were a common form of commercial deceit in the ancient world, and this proverb calls it an abomination to the Lord. God's holiness extends into the smallest transactions, revealing that integrity in hidden details reflects the character of God Himself.

text: Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;
digest: {firstname}, Paul catalogs real suffering, persecuted and struck down, yet insists believers are never forsaken or destroyed. This is the theology of the cross: apparent defeat coexists with the certainty of God's preserving power.

text: Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass.
digest: {firstname}, "commit" here carries the sense of rolling a burden onto the Lord entirely, an act of faith that releases outcomes to His sovereign will. The promise that follows, "he shall bring it to pass," rests on God's faithfulness, not the psalmist's effort.

text: The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb contrasts empty desire with diligence that is "made fat," or satisfied. Scripture consistently ties godly diligence to blessing, not because labor earns grace, but because it reflects a wisdom that honors God's created order.

text: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
digest: {firstname}, this exhortation follows Paul's extended defense of the bodily resurrection, and it is grounded there: because death is conquered, labor for the Lord is never in vain. Steadfastness in Christian work is theologically anchored in resurrection hope, not mere optimism.

text: The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb contrasts diligent planning with hasty action, associating the former with plenty and the latter with want. Wisdom literature consistently values patient, careful stewardship over impulsive shortcuts.

text: Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus commands visible good works, but the stated purpose is that observers glorify the Father in heaven, not the doer. Good works in Scripture always terminate in God's glory, never in human praise.

text: Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
digest: {firstname}, this psalm of Solomon insists that without the Lord's active building and watching, human labor is vain, regardless of effort. All legitimate human enterprise depends entirely on divine sustaining grace to have any lasting value.

text: Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
digest: {firstname}, this call to know well the state of one's flocks reflects the wisdom tradition's emphasis on faithful stewardship of what is entrusted. Diligent attention to one's responsibilities is itself a form of godly wisdom, not mere practicality.

text: But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
digest: {firstname}, this promise follows a chapter proclaiming God's incomparable greatness over the nations and the created order. Renewed strength is given specifically to those who wait on this transcendent, all-powerful God, not to those relying on their own resources.

text: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him.
digest: {firstname}, James describes God as giving generously and without reproach, meaning the request for wisdom is never met with divine irritation. This reflects the doctrine of God's generous character; asking in faith, without doubting, is the posture James commends.

text: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb observes the relational power of gentle speech versus provocative words. Wisdom literature repeatedly ties self-controlled speech to godliness, since the tongue reveals the state of the heart.

text: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus teaches this in the context of stewardship of worldly wealth, linking faithfulness in the least to trustworthiness in much. This principle underlies the doctrine of Christian stewardship: character is consistent, not compartmentalized by the size of the trust given.

text: For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister.
digest: {firstname}, the author assures believers that God, being just, does not forget labor done "for his name," specifically service rendered to fellow believers. Assurance of salvation here is tied to visible fruit that flows from genuine faith, evidence God Himself remembers.

text: And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
digest: {firstname}, this is Moses' prayer, asking that the Lord's favor rest upon human work and that He Himself establish it. Even the most sincere labor requires God's active establishing grace to have any enduring significance.

text: A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches, and loving favour rather than silver and gold.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb ranks a good name and God's favor above riches, reflecting the wisdom tradition's consistent priority of character over wealth. Reputation built on righteousness is treated as a more valuable inheritance than material gain.

text: Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
digest: {firstname}, Paul commands believers to replace anxiety with prayer, supplication, and thanksgiving, addressed directly to God. The peace that follows, described just after this verse, is a guarding peace that transcends understanding, granted by God in response to this kind of prayer.

text: Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
digest: {firstname}, lying lips are called an abomination to the Lord, while those who deal truly are His delight, showing that truthfulness reflects God's own unchanging character. Deceit is not merely socially harmful in Scripture; it is morally offensive to a holy God.

text: Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus issues this invitation specifically to the weary and burdened, offering rest that His yoke, described as easy and light, provides. This rest is found in submission to Christ's lordship, not in the absence of labor altogether.

text: Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
digest: {firstname}, Peter commands this casting of anxiety in the context of humbling oneself under God's mighty hand. The theological ground for casting our cares on Him is stated plainly: because He cares for us, His providence is trustworthy.

text: A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb holds human planning and divine sovereignty together without contradiction: a person plans, yet the Lord directs the steps. This reflects the doctrine of providence, where God's sovereign will governs even the details of human intention.

text: Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest.
digest: {firstname}, the Preacher's exhortation to work with all one's might arises from his sober reflection on mortality and the finality of the grave. Diligence in this life is urged precisely because there is no opportunity for labor or wisdom after death.

text: This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it.
digest: {firstname}, this day is declared to be one the Lord Himself has made, grounding rejoicing in God's sovereign ordaining of time itself. Joy in this psalm is a response to God's active work, not merely to favorable circumstances.

text: Not slothful in business; fervent in spirit; serving the Lord;
digest: {firstname}, Paul instructs believers to be fervent in spirit, explicitly "serving the Lord," tying zeal to its proper theological object. Diligence detached from serving Christ is not the virtue Paul commends here.

text: There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb acknowledges the multitude of human devices while affirming that only the Lord's counsel will ultimately stand. Human planning is real and legitimate, yet always subordinate to God's sovereign purpose.

text: For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
digest: {firstname}, Paul reminds Timothy that the Spirit given by God is one of power, love, and self-control, explicitly not fear. This verse grounds courage in the believer's reception of the Holy Spirit, a theological fact, not merely an emotional resolve.

text: Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
digest: {firstname}, "be still" in this psalm follows a description of God's power over nations and the earth's upheaval, a command to cease striving in light of His sovereignty. Knowing God rightly requires the stillness that recognizes His supremacy over every threat.

text: For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb distinguishes the righteous, who fall yet rise again, from the wicked, who fall into calamity. Perseverance through repeated failure, not sinless perfection, is presented here as a mark of genuine righteousness.

text: I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus establishes abiding in Him as the sole condition for spiritual fruitfulness, warning that apart from Him "ye can do nothing." This is a strong theological claim: all genuine spiritual fruit is Christ's work through the believer, not independent human effort.

text: In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb values substantive labor over empty talk, observing that "the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury." Wisdom literature consistently prizes tangible faithfulness over mere words about good intentions.

text: Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
digest: {firstname}, this promise of perfect peace is conditioned on a mind "stayed" on God, meaning fixed and resting on Him. Peace in Scripture is the fruit of sustained trust in God's character, not the absence of external trouble.

text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
digest: {firstname}, the prophet reduces true religion to justice, mercy, and humble walking with God, rejecting empty ritual sacrifice offered without these. This verse teaches that authentic covenant faithfulness is inseparable from ethical obedience flowing from a humble heart.

text: My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist locates his help specifically in "the maker of heaven and earth," a title asserting God's total sovereignty over creation. Confidence in God's help is grounded here in the doctrine of His creatorship, not in circumstantial reassurance.

text: He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb states plainly the connection between diligence and provision within God's ordered world. Wisdom literature affirms that laziness and poverty, diligence and increase, are linked by design, not coincidence.

text: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus calls this the summation of "the law and the prophets," meaning it distills the entire ethical demand of Scripture into reciprocal love. This is not merely good advice; Jesus presents it as the very heart of biblical righteousness toward others.

text: And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work:
digest: {firstname}, Paul's language of "all grace" and "all sufficiency in all things" is deliberately comprehensive, describing God's ability to supply believers for every good work. This generosity flows from grace, a theological reality, not from human merit or circumstance.

text: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb calls it folly and shame to answer before fully hearing a matter. Wisdom requires patient, complete understanding before response, reflecting the self-control that marks godly speech.

text: The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth; and with my song will I praise him.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's trust in the Lord as strength and shield produces both help and a resulting song of praise. Genuine trust in God, this psalm shows, naturally overflows into worship, not silent stoicism.

text: Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,
digest: {firstname}, the author pictures the Christian life as a race requiring the laying aside of both sin and encumbering weight, run "with patience." This endurance is possible because of the "cloud of witnesses" and, as the next verse says, by looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of faith.

text: A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb contrasts the fool, who vents his full mind, with the wise, who holds it back until later. Self-restraint in speech is here a marker of wisdom, reflecting mastery over one's own spirit.

text: In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.
digest: {firstname}, Paul commands giving thanks "in every thing," identifying this as God's will "in Christ Jesus concerning you." Thanksgiving in all circumstances flows from confidence in God's sovereign goodness, not from denial of hardship.

text: I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye.
digest: {firstname}, God promises instruction and guidance "with mine eye upon thee," language of attentive, personal care. This is a covenant promise of divine pedagogy, not abandonment to human guesswork.

text: A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb distinguishes the friend who loves at all times from the brother "born for adversity." Scripture values relationships tested and proven specifically in hardship as evidence of true loyalty.

text: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
digest: {firstname}, this commendation in the parable of the talents rewards faithfulness "over a few things" with greater trust and entrance into the master's joy. The theology here is that faithful stewardship of small responsibilities is what God rewards, not the size of the original portion.

text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord's nearness to the brokenhearted reflects His character toward the humble and contrite, a repeated theme throughout the Psalms. God draws near to weakness and brokenness, not to self-sufficiency.

text: The just man walketh in his integrity: his children are blessed after him.
digest: {firstname}, the righteous man's integrity is described as extending blessing to his children after him. This proverb reflects the covenantal principle that godly character has generational consequence.

text: And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's promise is precise: all things work together for good specifically for those who love God and are called according to His purpose. This is not a universal guarantee but a covenant promise rooted in God's sovereign purpose for His elect.

text: Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
digest: {firstname}, Paul instructs that speech should build up and minister grace "unto the hearers," part of his broader call to put off the old self and put on the new. Sanctified speech is evidence of the transformation the gospel produces in the believer.

text: Cause me to hear thy lovingkindness in the morning; for in thee do I trust: cause me to know the way wherein I should walk; for I lift up my soul unto thee.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist asks to hear God's lovingkindness "in the morning," paired with trust and a request to know the way to walk. Guidance and assurance of God's covenant love are sought together here, inseparably.

text: A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb compares a fitly spoken word to gold set in silver, prizing wisdom that discerns the right moment for speech. Timeliness in truthful speech is presented as its own form of wisdom.

text: When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.
digest: {firstname}, God speaks this to Israel in exile, promising His presence through waters and fire, not exemption from them. This reflects the doctrine of God's covenant faithfulness sustaining His people through, not around, trial.

text: Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.
digest: {firstname}, the heart is called the source, or "issues," of life, meaning all outward conduct flows from its condition. Guarding the heart above all else reflects the wisdom tradition's understanding that inner righteousness precedes outward obedience.

text: Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus ties generous giving to a generous return, "good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over." This teaches that the measure of grace and generosity one extends reflects, and is met by, the measure one receives from God.

text: I have set the LORD always before me: because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.
digest: {firstname}, setting the Lord always before him is what the psalmist credits for being unmoved, a posture of continual awareness of God's presence. This constancy is what grounds stability amid circumstance.

text: Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded.
digest: {firstname}, this exhortation to Asa's reforms promises reward for work, spoken through the prophet Azariah after describing seasons without the true God and without law. Faithfulness to covenant obedience is rewarded even after periods of national unfaithfulness.

text: A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb contrasts the faithful man, who abounds with blessing, with the one hastening to be rich, who "shall not be innocent." Scripture consistently warns that haste toward wealth endangers integrity.

text: Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus distinguishes His peace explicitly from the world's, given in the context of His promise of the Holy Spirit as Comforter. This peace is a fruit of Christ's finished work and abiding presence, not the product of favorable circumstances.

text: Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's soul waits "only" upon God, a deliberate exclusivity that rules out divided trust. Salvation is described here as coming from a single, sufficient source: God alone.

text: Honour the LORD with thy substance, and with the firstfruits of all thine increase:
digest: {firstname}, honoring the Lord with the "firstfruits" reflects the Old Testament principle of offering God priority, not merely leftovers. This proverb teaches that worship is measured by what comes first, not what remains.

text: And whatsoever ye do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God and the Father by him.
digest: {firstname}, Paul extends the lordship of Christ over "whatsoever ye do in word or deed," commanding it be done in His name with thanksgiving to God the Father. This total claim reflects the doctrine of Christ's comprehensive lordship over the whole of life.

text: And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?
digest: {firstname}, Nehemiah refuses to be drawn away from rebuilding the wall, discerning his opponents' request as a distraction from God's assigned work. Faithful discernment recognizes which demands on our attention serve God's purposes and which merely appear urgent.

text: Grant thee according to thine own heart, and fulfil all thy counsel.
digest: {firstname}, this is a corporate prayer, likely for the king before battle, asking God to grant the desire of his heart and fulfill his counsel. Intercessory prayer for another's God-honoring purposes reflects covenant solidarity among God's people.

text: He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb ties slowness to wrath with great understanding, and hastiness of spirit with folly. Self-control in the face of provocation is here identified as a mark of wisdom rooted in understanding, not mere temperament.

text: Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus confines each day's trouble to itself, teaching this immediately after commanding believers to seek first the kingdom of God. Trust in the Father's provision, established earlier in the passage, is what frees a disciple from anxious anticipation of tomorrow.

text: Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
digest: {firstname}, Paul extends the glory of God even to eating and drinking, the most ordinary acts, within a broader discussion of Christian liberty and love for others. No activity, however mundane, falls outside the believer's calling to glorify God.

text: The LORD will perfect that which concerneth me: thy mercy, O LORD, endureth for ever: forsake not the works of thine own hands.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist trusts God to "perfect that which concerneth me," appealing explicitly to God's enduring mercy, not his own merit or effort. Confidence in God's ongoing sanctifying work rests entirely on His covenant faithfulness.

text: The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb states that the liberal soul "shall be made fat," and the one who waters others is watered himself. Generosity, in the wisdom tradition, is not diminishment but the very means by which one is enriched.

text: And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it, when ye turn to the right hand, and when ye turn to the left.
digest: {firstname}, this promise of hearing a word behind you, directing the way, comes amid Isaiah's rebuke of Israel's misplaced trust in Egypt rather than the Lord. True guidance is available to those who turn from self-reliant alliances to trust in God's instruction.

text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
digest: {firstname}, this fruit is described in the singular, one unified fruit of the Spirit encompassing love, joy, peace, and more, set against the preceding list of the flesh's works. These qualities are the organic result of the Spirit's indwelling, not achievements pursued independently.

text: Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.
digest: {firstname}, casting one's burden upon the Lord comes with the promise that He will sustain and never allow the righteous to be permanently shaken. This is covenant assurance: the righteous may be tested but not ultimately overthrown.

text: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
digest: {firstname}, ruling one's own spirit is compared favorably to the mighty conquest of a city, elevating internal self-mastery above external victory. Scripture prizes godly self-control as a greater strength than military might.

text: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
digest: {firstname}, Paul writes this near his execution, describing the fight fought, the course finished, and the faith kept, followed immediately by his confidence in the crown of righteousness laid up for him. Endurance to the end is vindicated by the certain reward the righteous Judge will give.

text: My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist directs his voice to the Lord in the morning and then "looks up," an expectant posture of watching for God's response. Prayer here is not mere petition but attentive waiting for the Lord to act.

text: Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
digest: {firstname}, iron sharpening iron pictures the necessary friction of one person's countenance sharpening another's. Sanctifying growth within the community of believers often requires honest, even uncomfortable, mutual engagement.

text: Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's prayer ties joy and peace to believing, with hope abounding specifically "through the power of the Holy Ghost." Hope in this doxology is explicitly the Spirit's supernatural work, not a naturally generated feeling.

text: They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.
digest: {firstname}, this declaration of God's new mercies arises from the middle of Jeremiah's lament over Jerusalem's destruction, the darkest chapter in the book. Even amid covenant judgment, God's steadfast love and faithfulness remain the ground of hope.

text: Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb instructs against wearing oneself out to be rich, urging the wisdom to "cease from thine own wisdom" in that pursuit. Scripture warns that self-directed pursuit of wealth is itself a form of foolishness needing restraint.

text: Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing.
digest: {firstname}, gladness and singing mark the proper approach into God's presence, part of this psalm's call to worship the Lord as Creator and covenant God. Worship flows from recognizing whose we are, not mere obligation.

text: As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.
digest: {firstname}, Peter calls believers to steward their spiritual gifts as "good stewards of the manifold grace of God," for the benefit of others. Every gift is entrusted grace, meant to serve the body of Christ, not to be hoarded.

text: Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction.
digest: {firstname}, this instruction to speak for those unable to speak for themselves comes within the description of a virtuous life taught by a king's mother. Advocacy for the vulnerable is presented here as a mark of righteous, wise character.

text: And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works:
digest: {firstname}, this call to "consider one another" comes just before the exhortation not to forsake gathering together, tying mutual encouragement to the corporate life of the church. Provoking one another to love and good works is a communal, not merely individual, responsibility.

text: The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way.
digest: {firstname}, the steps of a good man being "ordered by the LORD," with God delighting in his way, ties divine providence to genuine relational pleasure. God is not a distant orderer of events but One who delights in the walk of the righteous.

text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:
digest: {firstname}, the Preacher's catalog of appointed times reflects his broader theme that God has ordained a fitting time for everything under heaven, even when human beings cannot discern it. Trusting God's sovereign timing, not forcing our own, is the wisdom this book commends.

text: Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
digest: {firstname}, Jesus' words about the plentiful harvest and few laborers come immediately after He is described as moved with compassion for crowds "as sheep having no shepherd." This compassion for the lost is the theological motive behind the call to pray for laborers that follows.

text: The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb warns that the fool's way is "right in his own eyes," a self-deception that only the willingness to hear counsel can correct. Wisdom requires humility to recognize the limits of one's own perspective.

text: Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD.
digest: {firstname}, waiting on the Lord, repeated twice for emphasis, is joined here with strength of heart, part of a psalm that opens by declaring the Lord as light and salvation. Courageous waiting flows from confidence already established in who God is.

text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:
digest: {firstname}, James rebukes presumptuous planning that ignores dependence on God's will, teaching believers to say "if the Lord will" rather than assuming control over the future. This reflects the doctrine of God's sovereignty over time and circumstance, against human self-sufficiency.

text: Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established.
digest: {firstname}, this proverb credits a multitude of counselors with establishing plans that would otherwise be disappointed. Wisdom literature consistently commends seeking counsel as a safeguard against the limits of individual judgment.

text: And the LORD shall guide thee continually, and satisfy thy soul in drought, and make fat thy bones: and thou shalt be like a watered garden, and like a spring of water, whose waters fail not.
digest: {firstname}, this promise of continual guidance follows God's call, earlier in the chapter, to true fasting marked by justice and mercy toward the oppressed. Covenant blessing and sustenance flow from obedience rooted in genuine righteousness, not empty religious observance.

text: He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
digest: {firstname}, dwelling in the "secret place of the most High" leads to abiding under the shadow of the Almighty, imagery of intimate, chosen nearness to God. This psalm goes on to describe specific protections that flow from this abiding relationship.

text: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise:
digest: {firstname}, the ant is commended for working without overseer or ruler, held up as a rebuke to the sluggard addressed throughout this passage. Diligence that requires no external compulsion reflects internalized wisdom.

text: And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
digest: {firstname}, God's answer to Paul's thrice-repeated prayer for the thorn's removal was not removal but the sufficiency of grace, with strength "made perfect in weakness." This teaches that divine power is displayed, not hindered, through human weakness surrendered to God.

text: But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus commands simple truthfulness, "yea, yea; nay, nay," within His broader teaching against oaths in the Sermon on the Mount. Anything beyond plain truthfulness, He says, comes from evil, exposing the corrupting effect of needing to swear to be believed.

text: For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly.
digest: {firstname}, God as "sun and shield" gives grace and glory, withholding no good thing from those who walk uprightly. This is covenant blessing extended specifically to those in right relationship with Him, not indiscriminate provision.

text: He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.
digest: {firstname}, kindness to the poor is described as lending directly to the Lord, who will repay the giver. This proverb grounds care for the poor in God's own commitment to reward such mercy.

text: And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;
digest: {firstname}, Paul says believers "glory in tribulations," explaining in the following verses that tribulation produces patience, character, and hope, a hope that does not disappoint because of the Holy Spirit's outpoured love. Suffering is theologically productive in the believer's sanctification, not merely endured.

text: NUN. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.
digest: {firstname}, God's word as lamp and light is stated within the longest psalm, an extended meditation on the sufficiency and authority of Scripture for guidance. The image of limited but sufficient light reflects Scripture's role in progressive, step-by-step obedience.

text: Wealth gotten by vanity shall be diminished: but he that gathereth by labour shall increase.
digest: {firstname}, wealth gained by vanity, or by hasty and dishonest means, diminishes, while wealth gathered by labor increases. This proverb values patient, honest labor as the legitimate means of increase under God's ordered creation.

text: For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
digest: {firstname}, Paul specifies it is the "love of money," not money itself, that is a root of all kinds of evil, warning that this love has caused some to err from the faith. The danger named here is idolatrous desire, a matter of the heart's ultimate loyalty.

text: The LORD is nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord's nearness to all who call upon Him "in truth" qualifies the promise: sincerity, not mere ritual invocation, is what this verse commends. This psalm as a whole celebrates God's greatness and goodness toward all He has made.

text: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
digest: {firstname}, acknowledging God "in all thy ways," not merely religious ones, is what leads Him to direct one's paths, continuing the theme begun two verses earlier about trusting Him with all the heart. Comprehensive submission to God's lordship over every area of life is in view here.

text: These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus promises peace and predicts tribulation in the same breath, within His final teaching to the disciples before the cross. He grounds their peace in His own conquest of the world, a victory secured through His death and resurrection.

text: Be of good courage, and he shall strengthen your heart, all ye that hope in the LORD.
digest: {firstname}, courage and strength of heart are promised to "all ye that hope in the LORD," closing a psalm that moves from deep distress to renewed trust. Hope in God's covenant faithfulness is the basis for sustained courage through affliction.

text: He that walketh uprightly walketh surely: but he that perverteth his ways shall be known.
digest: {firstname}, walking uprightly brings security, while perverse ways will eventually be exposed. This proverb reflects the wisdom tradition's confidence that righteousness and deceit lead to inherently different, discoverable outcomes.

text: With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men:
digest: {firstname}, Paul instructs bondservants to serve with goodwill "as to the Lord, and not to men," part of his household code grounding all relationships in service to Christ. Ultimate motivation for service is always theological, directed toward Christ regardless of the immediate human authority.

text: My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist, after nearly stumbling over the prosperity of the wicked, confesses that even as flesh and heart fail, God remains his strength and portion forever. This resolution comes only after entering God's sanctuary, where eternal perspective is restored.

text: Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
digest: {firstname}, diligence in one's work bringing a person "before kings" reflects the wisdom tradition's confidence that skillful, faithful labor is eventually recognized. This is presented as the natural outworking of diligence within God's ordered world.

text: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus states that the heart follows treasure, spoken within His teaching against storing up earthly treasure and for storing up treasure in heaven. Where ultimate value is placed reveals, and shapes, the true orientation of the heart.

text: I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's patient waiting precedes God's inclining to him and hearing his cry, part of a psalm that moves from the pit of despair to a new song of praise. Patient endurance in prayer, not immediate resolution, precedes the deliverance described here.

text: The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going.
digest: {firstname}, the simple believes every word, while the prudent considers his steps carefully. This proverb commends discernment as protection against being led astray by every claim presented.

text: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
digest: {firstname}, Paul's definition of love, patient and kind, not envious or boastful, comes within his argument that spiritual gifts without love profit nothing. Love is defined here by concrete character and action, the theological standard against which all gifts and service are measured.

text: For his anger endureth but a moment; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning.
digest: {firstname}, momentary anger giving way to lifelong favor, and weeping to morning joy, is set within a psalm of thanksgiving for deliverance from near death. God's discipline is temporary, but His covenant favor toward His people is enduring.

text: Man's goings are of the LORD; how can a man then understand his own way?
digest: {firstname}, this proverb acknowledges that a person's steps are of the Lord, questioning how anyone could fully understand their own way. Human self-understanding is limited precisely because ultimate direction belongs to God's sovereign ordering.

text: Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
digest: {firstname}, contentment is grounded explicitly in God's promise, quoted from the Old Testament, never to leave or forsake His people. This covenant promise, not circumstance, is the theological basis for freedom from the love of money mentioned in the same verse.

text: The counsel of the LORD standeth for ever, the thoughts of his heart to all generations.
digest: {firstname}, the counsel of the Lord standing forever, His thoughts to all generations, is set against the futility of nations' plans described earlier in this psalm. God's eternal purpose transcends every temporal scheme of man.

text: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
digest: {firstname}, pride preceding destruction and a haughty spirit preceding a fall reflects the wisdom tradition's consistent warning against self-exaltation. This proverb functions as both observation and warning about the moral order God has built into creation.

text: And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus warns against covetousness immediately after refusing to arbitrate an inheritance dispute, teaching that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. This precedes the parable of the rich fool, whose error was trusting in accumulated wealth rather than being "rich toward God."

text: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's peaceful sleep rests on the Lord alone making him "dwell in safety," closing a psalm that begins with a cry for God's mercy amid distress. Security here is entirely dependent on God's providential care, not on circumstances being free of threat.

text: Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
digest: {firstname}, the absence of counsel leads to a people's fall, while safety is found in a multitude of counselors. This proverb repeatedly emphasizes communal wisdom as a check on the limits of individual understanding.

text: And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
digest: {firstname}, Paul contrasts conformity to this present age with transformation by a renewed mind, given as the pathway to discerning God's good, acceptable, and perfect will. This renewal is the outworking of the mercies of God described at the start of the chapter, not self-improvement.

text: Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist invites God to search his heart, following an extended meditation on God's omniscience and omnipresence throughout the psalm. Genuine self-examination submits to God's searching knowledge rather than relying on self-assessment alone.

text: If thou faint in the day of adversity, thy strength is small.
digest: {firstname}, fainting in adversity reveals that strength was small to begin with, according to this proverb. Trials expose, rather than create, the true condition of one's inner fortitude.

text: But ye, brethren, be not weary in well doing.
digest: {firstname}, Paul urges believers not to grow weary in well-doing within a passage addressing those who were idle and disorderly in the church. Steady faithfulness in doing right is commanded even where surrounding examples might discourage it.

text: Shew me thy ways, O LORD; teach me thy paths.
digest: {firstname}, the request to be shown God's ways and taught His paths is part of an acrostic psalm built around confession, trust, and covenant instruction. Teachability before God is the posture this entire psalm models.

text: The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility.
digest: {firstname}, the fear of the Lord as the "instruction of wisdom" and humility preceding honor reflects the wisdom tradition's foundational principle established already in Proverbs 1:7. Reverence for God, not intellectual achievement, is the beginning point of true wisdom.

text: But it shall not be so among you: but whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister;
digest: {firstname}, Jesus redefines greatness as service in response to the disciples' dispute over status, teaching that whoever would be great must become a servant. This inversion of worldly greatness is grounded in His own example, stated in the following verses, of coming to serve and give His life as a ransom.

text: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
digest: {firstname}, the command to "forget not all his benefits" follows the psalmist's self-address to bless the Lord, part of an extended recounting of God's forgiveness, healing, and covenant love. Deliberate remembrance of God's works is presented as an act of worship against the natural tendency to forget.

text: Heaviness in the heart of man maketh it stoop: but a good word maketh it glad.
digest: {firstname}, heaviness weighing down the heart, countered by a good word that makes it glad, reflects the wisdom tradition's attention to the real power of speech to affect another's inner state. Encouraging words are treated as genuinely restorative, not merely pleasant.

text: For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD.
digest: {firstname}, God's declaration that His thoughts and ways exceed ours comes within His invitation to the thirsty and the wicked to return to Him, promising abundant pardon. His transcendence is the ground for trusting His mercy even when it exceeds human expectation.

text: O give thanks unto the LORD, for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
digest: {firstname}, thanksgiving is called for because the Lord is good and His mercy "endureth for ever," opening a psalm that recounts God's deliverance of His people from various distresses. Praise here is rooted in God's unchanging covenant character, demonstrated repeatedly through His redemptive acts.

text: He that followeth after righteousness and mercy findeth life, righteousness, and honour.
digest: {firstname}, following after righteousness and mercy is what leads to life, righteousness, and honor, according to this proverb. Pursuit of these qualities, not mere admiration of them, is what the wisdom tradition credits with producing genuine reward.

text: My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.
digest: {firstname}, John's call to love "in deed and in truth," not merely in word, comes within his broader test of genuine faith by its fruit of active love for fellow believers. Assurance before God, described later in the same passage, is tied to this tangible evidence of love.

text: Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's self-directed question, why his soul is downcast, followed by the command to hope in God, is repeated as a refrain throughout this psalm of spiritual longing. Faith here includes honest lament held together with deliberate, repeated resolve to hope.

text: The heart of the prudent getteth knowledge; and the ear of the wise seeketh knowledge.
digest: {firstname}, the heart of the prudent getting knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeking it, reflects wisdom's active, ongoing pursuit rather than passive possession. Genuine wisdom continually seeks understanding rather than resting content with what it already knows.

text: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;
digest: {firstname}, Paul instructs believers, as "the elect of God, holy and beloved," to put on mercy, kindness, humility, and patience. These virtues are commanded on the basis of the believer's identity in Christ, not as a means of earning that identity.

text: Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
digest: {firstname}, David's request for a clean heart and renewed spirit comes from his psalm of repentance after his sin with Bathsheba, acknowledging he cannot produce this renewal himself. Genuine repentance depends entirely on God's regenerating grace, not self-reformation.

text: He that trusteth in his own heart is a fool: but whoso walketh wisely, he shall be delivered.
digest: {firstname}, trusting one's own heart is called foolish, while walking wisely brings deliverance. This proverb reflects the biblical assessment of the human heart as unreliable apart from wisdom drawn from God.

text: Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus calls peacemakers, not merely the peaceable, "the children of God," part of the Beatitudes describing the character of kingdom citizens. Active peacemaking reflects the character of God Himself, who reconciles sinners to Himself through Christ.

text: O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is;
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's soul thirsting for God "in a dry and thirsty land" was written, according to the superscription, while David was in the wilderness of Judah. Earnest seeking of God is intensified, not diminished, by physical and circumstantial desolation.

text: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
digest: {firstname}, a merry heart as good medicine, contrasted with a broken spirit that dries the bones, reflects wisdom literature's serious regard for the connection between inner disposition and outward wellbeing. Emotional and spiritual health are treated here as genuinely consequential, not incidental.

text: (For we walk by faith, not by sight:)
digest: {firstname}, walking by faith and not by sight is stated within Paul's discussion of the believer's confidence despite being "absent from the body" and awaiting the resurrection. Faith trusts realities not yet visibly confirmed, grounded in the certainty of what God has promised.

text: Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name.
digest: {firstname}, the request to be taught God's way, to walk in His truth, and for an undivided heart comes from a psalm of David in distress, appealing to God's mercy and truth. A divided heart is named explicitly here as an obstacle requiring God's own unifying work to overcome.

text: Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning.
digest: {firstname}, giving instruction to a wise man making him wiser still reflects the wisdom tradition's principle that teachability, not achieved status, marks continued growth in wisdom. Wisdom is never a completed possession in this proverb's view.

text: Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
digest: {firstname}, bearing one another's burdens is said to fulfill "the law of Christ," within Paul's instruction to restore a fallen brother with gentleness. Mutual burden-bearing is presented as the practical expression of Christ's own law of love.

text: O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
digest: {firstname}, tasting and seeing that the Lord is good, with blessing pronounced on the one who trusts Him, comes from a psalm David wrote after feigning madness before Abimelech. Experiential trust in God's goodness is commended even, or especially, after deliverance from self-inflicted danger.

text: Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge.
digest: {firstname}, applying the heart to instruction and the ear to knowledge requires deliberate, active attention, part of this chapter's repeated counsel to a son. Wisdom is received through disciplined engagement, not passive proximity to good teaching.

text: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
digest: {firstname}, sanctifying Christ as Lord in the heart precedes readiness to give a reasoned defense of one's hope, done "with meekness and fear," within Peter's instruction on suffering for righteousness' sake. Apologetic readiness flows from prior submission to Christ's lordship, not mere argumentative skill.

text: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's declaration of unity's goodness and pleasantness is followed by the image of oil running down Aaron's beard and dew descending on Zion, both signs of God's consecrating blessing. Unity among God's covenant people is portrayed as a place where the Lord commands blessing.

text: Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
digest: {firstname}, boasting about tomorrow is foolish, since no one knows what a day will bring, a warning consistent with the wisdom tradition's emphasis on human limitation before God's sovereignty over time. Confidence about the future belongs properly to God alone.

text: Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?
digest: {firstname}, Peter's question about forgiving seven times, likely thinking this generous, is met by Jesus' answer of seventy times seven, followed immediately by the parable of the unforgiving servant. Limitless forgiveness reflects the immeasurable forgiveness believers themselves have received from God.

text: Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer.
digest: {firstname}, the request that both words and heart meditation be acceptable to the Lord closes a psalm celebrating God's revelation in creation and in His perfect law. Right speech flows from a heart already shaped by meditation on God's revealed truth.

text: Pleasant words are as an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones.
digest: {firstname}, pleasant words compared to honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones, reflects the wisdom tradition's high regard for gracious speech as genuinely beneficial, not merely polite. Words carry real, almost physical, power to heal or wound.

text: So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.
digest: {firstname}, every person giving account of themselves to God is stated within Paul's instruction against judging fellow believers over disputable matters. Personal accountability before God, not comparison to others, is the proper measure of one's own conduct.

text: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.
digest: {firstname}, God healing the brokenhearted and binding their wounds appears within a psalm celebrating His power over creation alongside His tender care for the afflicted. The same God who names the stars attends personally to the brokenhearted.

text: Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins.
digest: {firstname}, hatred stirring up strife, contrasted with love that covers all sins, reflects wisdom's understanding of how relational postures either multiply or absorb conflict. Love's covering here anticipates the greater covering accomplished through Christ's atonement.

text: Let all your things be done with charity.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's closing instruction, that all things be done in love, summarizes much of what he has taught throughout the letter, especially his teaching on love in chapter thirteen. Love is meant to govern every action within the life of the church.

text: Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.
digest: {firstname}, resting in the Lord and waiting patiently, set against fretting over the prosperity of the wicked, is a repeated theme throughout this wisdom psalm. Peace flows from trusting God's justice will prevail in His own timing, not from present circumstances being resolved.

text: Better is little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble therewith.
digest: {firstname}, a little with the fear of the Lord being better than great treasure with trouble reflects the wisdom tradition's consistent ranking of reverence for God above material abundance. Peace with God is valued above wealth that compromises that relationship.

text: Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation.
digest: {firstname}, this declaration of trust without fear, because God has become salvation, is part of a hymn of praise Isaiah anticipates Israel singing on the day of restoration. Confident trust flows from God's accomplished salvation, not merely the absence of present threat.

text: For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's hope and trust traced back to his youth reflects a psalm written, likely, in old age, pleading for continued deliverance. A lifelong pattern of trust in God is the ground for confidence in His continued faithfulness.

text: Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it.
digest: {firstname}, withholding good from those it is due, when it is within one's power to give, is warned against within this chapter's broader instruction on wisdom's practical fruits. Active kindness, not passive good intentions, is what wisdom requires.

text: Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.
digest: {firstname}, faith defined as "the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen" introduces the great catalog of Old Testament believers who followed God's promises. This definition frames faith as confident assurance grounded in God's character, not wishful thinking.

text: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
digest: {firstname}, God as refuge and strength, "a very present help in trouble," opens a psalm that goes on to describe cosmic upheaval met by God's unshaken city and presence. His help is immediate and constant, not distant or occasional.

text: A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.
digest: {firstname}, a sound heart as life to the body, contrasted with envy as rottenness to the bones, reflects wisdom's attention to how inner disposition affects the whole person. Envy is treated here as corrosive at the deepest level.

text: Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus' assurance of being "of more value than many sparrows" comes within His instruction to the twelve before sending them out, addressing fear of persecution. Human worth is assigned by the Father's providential care, extending even to sparrows, not by circumstance or opposition.

text: He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord restoring the soul and leading in righteous paths "for his name's sake" ties the Shepherd's guidance to His own covenant reputation, not merely the sheep's benefit. God's faithfulness to His own name secures the believer's guidance and restoration.

text: He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.
digest: {firstname}, a person without rule over their own spirit is compared to a broken-down city without walls. Self-control is treated here as essential defense, without which a person is left exposed to every incursion.

text: Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.
digest: {firstname}, God's comfort in tribulation is given so believers may comfort others in similar trouble, part of Paul's opening praise of "the God of all comfort" after describing his own severe affliction in Asia. Suffering and comfort received from God are meant to be extended to others, not retained.

text: A good man sheweth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion.
digest: {firstname}, the good man who shows favor and lends, guiding affairs with discretion, is part of an acrostic psalm describing the blessed life of one who fears the Lord. Generosity paired with wisdom reflects the integrated righteousness this psalm commends.

text: The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression.
digest: {firstname}, discretion making a person slow to anger, with passing over transgression called their glory, reflects the wisdom tradition's high esteem for restraint in the face of offense. Overlooking wrongs is treated as strength, not weakness.

text: Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's instruction to look also on the interests of others introduces the great Christological hymn that follows, describing Christ's self-emptying humility. This other-centered posture is grounded in, and modeled after, Christ's own example.

text: For thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee.
digest: {firstname}, eating the labor of one's hands with happiness is described as blessing within this psalm celebrating the flourishing household of one who fears the Lord. Enjoyment of honest labor's fruit is presented as covenant blessing, not something to feel guilty about.

text: He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.
digest: {firstname}, walking with wise people producing wisdom, while companionship with fools brings destruction, reflects wisdom's serious regard for the shaping power of one's associations. Character is formed, this proverb warns, largely by the company one keeps.

text: By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus names love for one another as the identifying mark of His disciples, spoken immediately after washing the disciples' feet and giving the new commandment to love as He loved them. Christlike, sacrificial love, not doctrinal correctness alone, is the sign Jesus assigns to genuine discipleship.

text: Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the LORD hath dealt bountifully with thee.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's command to his own soul to "return unto thy rest" follows his testimony of God's deliverance from death, tears, and stumbling. Rest here is a remembered covenant reality to return to, grounded in God's proven bountiful dealing.

text: Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles.
digest: {firstname}, guarding the mouth and tongue as protection from trouble reflects the wisdom tradition's repeated warnings about the tongue's power to harm. Self-controlled speech is treated as essential safeguarding of one's soul.

text: And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper.
digest: {firstname}, the blessed man's likeness to a tree planted by rivers, bearing fruit in season, is set against the wicked's fate as chaff in this opening psalm of the Psalter. Being "planted," rooted deliberately in meditation on God's law described earlier in the psalm, is what produces this steady fruitfulness.

text: The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them.
digest: {firstname}, the integrity of the upright guiding them, while the crookedness of the treacherous destroys them, reflects wisdom's confidence that character functions as an internal compass. Integrity and destruction are set as natural consequences flowing from the heart's condition.

text: No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus' declaration that no one can serve two masters, naming God and mammon specifically, closes His teaching on treasure and the eye as the lamp of the body. Undivided allegiance to God is not optional in Jesus' teaching; competing ultimate loyalties are called impossible.

text: The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
digest: {firstname}, the accumulation of images, rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, horn of salvation, high tower, opens a psalm of thanksgiving David composed after deliverance from Saul and all his enemies. This piling of metaphors reflects the comprehensiveness of God's proven, experienced protection.

text: The hand of the diligent shall bear rule: but the slothful shall be under tribute.
digest: {firstname}, the diligent hand ruling, while the slothful is put to forced labor, reflects wisdom's consistent linking of diligence to freedom and laziness to bondage. This proverb frames diligence as itself a form of wise stewardship God honors.

text: What shall we then say to these things? If God be for us, who can be against us?
digest: {firstname}, Paul's rhetorical question, "if God be for us, who can be against us," follows his declaration that nothing can separate believers from God's love, grounded in Christ's death, resurrection, and intercession. Confidence here rests entirely on God's demonstrated commitment to His elect through Christ.

text: Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast.
digest: {firstname}, taking refuge under the shadow of God's wings "until these calamities be overpast" was written, according to its superscription, while David fled from Saul in a cave. This refuge is temporary shelter through trouble, not permanent removal from it.

text: Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right.
digest: {firstname}, even a child being known by their doings, whether pure and right, reflects the wisdom tradition's belief that character reveals itself early, regardless of age or experience. Genuine righteousness or its absence shows itself in conduct from the start.

text: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
digest: {firstname}, believers as God's "workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works," follows Paul's declaration that salvation is by grace through faith, "not of works," lest anyone should boast. Good works are the fruit of salvation by grace, prepared beforehand by God, never its cause.

text: Thy mercy, O LORD, is in the heavens; and thy faithfulness reacheth unto the clouds.
digest: {firstname}, God's mercy reaching to the heavens and faithfulness to the clouds is set against the wickedness of the transgressor described at this psalm's opening. The immensity of God's covenant love stands in stark contrast to the smallness of human sin.

text: Prepare thy work without, and make it fit for thyself in the field; and afterwards build thine house.
digest: {firstname}, preparing outside work before building one's house reflects the wisdom tradition's value of proper order: securing provision before pursuing comfort. Foundational diligence is commended over premature settling into ease.

text: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's charge to Timothy to study, rightly dividing "the word of truth," comes within his broader instruction to be a faithful workman unashamed before God. Careful, diligent handling of Scripture is a pastoral responsibility, not an optional pursuit.

text: Blessed be God, which hath not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me.
digest: {firstname}, blessing God for not turning away prayer or mercy closes a psalm recounting both God's testing of His people through fire and water and His bringing them "out into a wealthy place." Answered prayer here follows tested, refined faith, not untested ease.

text: He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the LORD, happy is he.
digest: {firstname}, handling a matter wisely leading to good, and trusting the Lord leading to happiness, places practical wisdom and personal trust in God side by side as complementary, not competing, virtues. Neither wise handling nor bare trust alone completes the picture; both together yield the blessing described.

text: And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise.
digest: {firstname}, the Golden Rule, doing to others as you would have them do to you, is given within Jesus' teaching on loving enemies and lending expecting nothing back. This ethic is grounded in reflecting the mercy of the Most High, described just after, who is kind even to the ungrateful.

text: In the multitude of my thoughts within me thy comforts delight my soul.
digest: {firstname}, God's comforts delighting the soul amid a multitude of anxious thoughts is set within a psalm crying out for justice against the wicked. Comfort here does not eliminate the anxious thoughts but meets and outweighs them through trust in God's coming justice.

text: By humility and the fear of the LORD are riches, and honour, and life.
digest: {firstname}, humility and the fear of the Lord together leading to riches, honor, and life, reflects the wisdom tradition's consistent pairing of reverence toward God with genuine flourishing. These outcomes flow from right relationship with God, not independent pursuit of them.

text: Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
digest: {firstname}, faithfulness required of stewards is stated within Paul's discussion of how the apostles ought to be regarded, as servants of Christ and stewards of God's mysteries. Faithfulness, not human judgment of success, is the standard by which stewards are ultimately assessed by the Lord.

text: From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.
digest: {firstname}, crying "from the end of the earth" when the heart is overwhelmed, asking to be led to a rock higher than oneself, reflects the psalmist's recognition that ultimate perspective must come from beyond his own vantage point. This request for God's transcendent stability answers the disorientation of being overwhelmed.

text: A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken.
digest: {firstname}, a merry heart producing a cheerful face, while sorrow of heart breaks the spirit, reflects wisdom literature's understanding that the heart's condition inevitably surfaces outwardly. Inner reality and outward expression are treated as deeply connected, not separable.

text: And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus' declaration that service to "the least of these my brethren" is service to Him comes within the parable of the sheep and the goats, describing final judgment. This collapses the distance between caring for the overlooked and serving Christ Himself, with eternal consequence attached.

text: I wait for the LORD, my soul doth wait, and in his word do I hope.
digest: {firstname}, waiting for the Lord, with the soul hoping specifically in His word, comes from a penitential psalm crying "out of the depths" for forgiveness. Hope here is anchored in God's revealed promise of redemption, not a vague feeling that circumstances will improve.

text: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
digest: {firstname}, covering sin leading to a lack of prosperity, while confessing and forsaking it leads to mercy, reflects the consistent biblical pattern that honest confession, not concealment, is the path to restoration. This anticipates the fuller gospel pattern of repentance leading to grace.

text: For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
digest: {firstname}, freedom not given as occasion for the flesh but for serving one another in love comes within Paul's argument against returning to bondage under the law while also warning against license. Christian liberty is bounded by love, never by legalism or by self-indulgence.

text: Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah.
digest: {firstname}, God "daily" loading His people with benefits is celebrated within a triumphant psalm depicting God's procession as victorious King among His people. Daily, ongoing generosity, not occasional blessing, characterizes God's covenant relationship with His own.

text: Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end.
digest: {firstname}, hearing counsel and receiving instruction now, so as to be wise "in thy latter end," reflects wisdom's long view: instruction accepted early yields fruit that only becomes fully visible later in life. Present teachability is an investment in future wisdom.

text: Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's care to provide honest things "not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men" comes within his instructions for handling the collection for the Jerusalem church with full accountability. Integrity includes visible transparency before others, not merely private conviction before God.

text: The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments: his praise endureth for ever.
