digest: {firstname}, the fear of the Lord as "the beginning of wisdom," with good understanding belonging to those who keep His commandments, closes this acrostic psalm celebrating God's works and covenant faithfulness. Wisdom's starting point is reverent obedience to God, not intellectual accomplishment.

text: Every prudent man dealeth with knowledge: but a fool layeth open his folly.
digest: {firstname}, every prudent person acting with knowledge, while a fool exposes his own folly, reflects wisdom's contrast between deliberate, informed action and careless self-exposure. Prudence conceals wisely; folly reveals itself without meaning to.

text: Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
digest: {firstname}, speech seasoned with grace, "as it were with salt," equipping one to answer every person rightly, closes Paul's instructions on prayer and conduct toward outsiders. Gracious speech is presented as essential to faithful gospel witness before a watching world.

text: I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.
digest: {firstname}, delighting to do God's will, with His law written within the heart, anticipates the New Covenant promise of an internalized law given through the Spirit. Obedience here flows from transformed desire, not mere external compulsion.

text: There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
digest: {firstname}, a way that seems right to a person but ends in death is a warning repeated again later in Proverbs, underscoring its importance to the wisdom tradition. Human perception of rightness is an unreliable guide apart from God's revealed truth.

text: Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
digest: {firstname}, the wise builder who hears Christ's words and does them, building on rock, closes the Sermon on the Mount with a warning about final judgment based on obedient response to His teaching. Hearing alone does not secure the foundation; doing is what withstands the storm of judgment.

text: For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord as good and ready to forgive, "plenteous in mercy to all them that call upon thee," reflects David's appeal within a prayer for God's help amid affliction. God's readiness to forgive, not reluctance, characterizes His covenant disposition toward those who call on Him.

text: A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself; but the simple pass on, and are punished.
digest: {firstname}, the prudent seeing evil and hiding themselves, while the simple suffer for pressing on, reflects wisdom's value of foresight as protective discernment. This kind of prudence is a quiet virtue, easily overlooked until its absence causes harm.

text: And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
digest: {firstname}, Paul's instruction to lead a quiet life, mind one's own business, and work with one's hands comes within his broader teaching on sanctification and love for the brotherhood. Faithful, ordinary steadiness is presented as its own form of obedience, not lesser than more visible callings.

text: The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
digest: {firstname}, the righteous flourishing like a palm tree and growing like a cedar in Lebanon, both known for deep-rooted, enduring strength, closes a psalm contrasting the righteous with the wicked's brief flourishing. Righteous growth is pictured as steady and lasting, sustained by being "planted in the house of the LORD," as the following verse says.

text: He that hath knowledge spareth his words: and a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit.
digest: {firstname}, one with knowledge sparing words, and a person of understanding remaining calm in spirit, reflects wisdom's connection between genuine understanding and self-controlled speech. Restraint here flows from depth of understanding, not mere reticence.

text: Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
digest: {firstname}, brotherly love and preferring one another in honor come within Paul's extended description of the transformed Christian life following his call to present bodies as living sacrifices. This mutual preferring of others runs directly against natural self-exaltation, reflecting Spirit-wrought humility.

text: In the day when I cried thou answeredst me, and strengthenedst me with strength in my soul.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's recollection that God answered and strengthened him "in the day when I cried" opens a psalm of thanksgiving that anticipates all the kings of the earth praising God's word. Remembered answered prayer builds confidence for future trust in God's continued faithfulness.

text: There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.
digest: {firstname}, speech like the piercing of a sword, contrasted with the healing tongue of the wise, reflects wisdom's serious regard for words as genuinely capable of wounding or healing. Speech is never neutral in this proverb's assessment.

text: But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.
digest: {firstname}, doing good and sharing, called a sacrifice well pleasing to God, closes the author's practical instructions following the great theological exposition of Christ's superior priesthood earlier in the letter. Generosity is framed here as an act of worship, an appropriate response to the sacrifice of Christ already described.

text: I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.
digest: {firstname}, seeking the Lord and being delivered from all fears, from the same psalm David wrote after feigning madness before Abimelech, ties genuine deliverance to genuine seeking. Fear is met and answered by God, not denied or suppressed.

text: Every purpose is established by counsel: and with good advice make war.
digest: {firstname}, every purpose established by counsel, with war to be made "by wise counsel," reflects wisdom's insistence that even decisive, weighty matters require careful, informed deliberation. Wisdom is never presented as instinctive alone; it requires sought input.

text: Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
digest: {firstname}, Peter's fourfold instruction, honor all, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king, comes within his teaching on Christian conduct amid a hostile society. These distinctions matter: fear belongs to God alone, while honor and love extend broadly to others, including civil authority.

text: Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
digest: {firstname}, fullness of joy in God's presence and pleasures forevermore at His right hand closes a psalm the New Testament applies to Christ's resurrection, since His soul was not left in Sheol. This joy is ultimately secured through the risen Christ, in whom this psalm finds its fullest meaning.

text: When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom.
digest: {firstname}, pride bringing shame, while wisdom accompanies the lowly, reflects the wisdom tradition's consistent pairing of humility with wisdom and pride with its own downfall. This proverb functions as both diagnosis and warning about the moral order God has established.

text: My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons.
digest: {firstname}, James warns against holding "the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ" with partiality, introducing his extended rebuke of favoritism toward the rich within the assembly. Genuine faith in the glorious Lord Jesus cannot coexist with the sin of favoritism toward some over others.

text: The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord's preservation of one's going out and coming in, "from this time forth, and even for evermore," closes a psalm celebrating God as keeper, one who neither slumbers nor sleeps. This covers the whole of ordinary life and its movements, sustained by God's unceasing watchfulness.

text: Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding.
digest: {firstname}, happiness belonging to the one who finds wisdom and gains understanding continues this chapter's extended praise of wisdom's value, described later as more precious than rubies. True happiness is tied here to rightly ordered understanding, not mere circumstance.

text: And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.
digest: {firstname}, going two miles when compelled to go one, within the Sermon on the Mount's teaching on non-retaliation, reflects Jesus' pattern of exceeding minimum obligation with generous, unexpected response. This goes beyond compliance into active goodwill toward one who has wronged you.

text: But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble.
digest: {firstname}, singing of God's power and mercy "in the morning" because He has been "my defence and refuge," was written, according to its superscription, while Saul's men watched David's house to kill him. Praise follows remembered deliverance even while danger still surrounds.

text: A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit.
digest: {firstname}, a person's pride bringing them low, while honor upholds the humble in spirit, reflects the consistent wisdom pattern reversing the world's expected order of exaltation. Humility, not self-promotion, is what this proverb credits with genuine, lasting honor.

text: Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;
digest: {firstname}, Paul's insistence that sufficiency to think anything as of ourselves comes not from us but from God comes within his discussion of the surpassing glory of the new covenant ministry. Even the capacity for right thought and ministry is credited entirely to God's enabling grace.

text: Delight thyself also in the LORD; and he shall give thee the desires of thine heart.
digest: {firstname}, delighting in the Lord leading Him to give the heart's desires continues this psalm's extended contrast between trusting God and fretting over evildoers' apparent success. Delight in God reorders desire itself, not merely secures whatever was already wanted.

text: A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.
digest: {firstname}, a friend who sticks closer than a brother, distinguished from many companions who may still lead to ruin, values depth of loyal friendship over its breadth. Scripture prizes proven, faithful companionship over wide but shallow association.

text: Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:
digest: {firstname}, Paul's confidence that God who began a good work will complete it "until the day of Jesus Christ" opens his letter with assurance rooted entirely in God's faithfulness to finish what He starts. Perseverance of the saints is grounded here in God's ongoing sanctifying work, not the believer's self-sustained effort.

text: Teach me to do thy will; for thou art my God: thy spirit is good; lead me into the land of uprightness.
digest: {firstname}, the request to be taught God's will and led by His good Spirit "into the land of uprightness" closes a psalm of urgent distress, appealing to God's righteousness and mercy. Even the desire to obey is something requested from God, not assumed to arise from oneself.

text: By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone.
digest: {firstname}, long patience persuading a ruler, and a soft tongue breaking a bone, reflects the wisdom tradition's confidence that gentleness accomplishes what force alone cannot. Patient, gentle persistence is credited with a genuinely persuasive power.

text: For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
digest: {firstname}, counting the cost before building a tower is one of two parables Jesus tells immediately after describing the total cost of discipleship, including forsaking all. Genuine discipleship, Jesus teaches, requires the same sober calculation as any serious undertaking, not impulsive commitment.

text: Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them.
digest: {firstname}, great peace belonging to those who love God's law, with "nothing shall offend them," reflects this psalm's extended celebration of Scripture's sufficiency for stability. Love for God's revealed word, not merely knowledge of it, produces this unshakable peace.

text: The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD.
digest: {firstname}, the heart's preparations belonging to a person, but the tongue's answer coming from the Lord, reflects a partnership between human intention and divine sovereignty even in speech. This proverb continues the chapter's theme of God's governance over human plans.

text: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's instruction to Timothy not to let his youth be despised, but to be an example in word, conduct, love, faith, and purity, reflects pastoral counsel that respect is earned through consistent godly character, not merely claimed by age or office. Timothy's authority as a young pastor rested on visible integrity, not title alone.

text: The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord's goodness to all, His tender mercies "over all his works," reflects this psalm's sweeping celebration of God's universal reign and compassion. This goodness extends to the whole created order, not merely to a select group.

text: In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
digest: {firstname}, sin not lacking in many words, while the one who restrains his lips is wise, reflects wisdom's consistent counsel that verbal restraint guards against sin's increase. Fewer words, carefully chosen, are treated here as evidence of wisdom.

text: Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.
digest: {firstname}, rendering to all what is due, tribute, custom, fear, and honor, comes within Paul's teaching on submission to governing authorities, established by God according to the earlier verses of this chapter. Civil obligations are treated as a matter of Christian integrity before God, who has ordained such authority.

text: The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
digest: {firstname}, the Lord as light and salvation, leading to the rhetorical question of whom to fear, opens a psalm that moves from confident trust to earnest petition amid enemies. Fear's grip is broken specifically by who God is revealed to be, not by the absence of genuine danger.

text: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
digest: {firstname}, training a child in the way he should go, with the promise he will not depart from it when old, reflects the wisdom tradition's confidence in the lasting power of early, deliberate formation. This proverb speaks to a general pattern of covenant nurture, not an unconditional guarantee independent of the child's own response.

text: Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal:
digest: {firstname}, the warning against storing treasures where moth, rust, and thieves take them opens Jesus' teaching that concludes with the impossibility of serving both God and money. What decays or can be stolen was never meant to hold the place only God's eternal kingdom deserves.

text: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
digest: {firstname}, the request to be taught to "number our days" so as to apply the heart to wisdom comes from Moses' prayer reflecting on human frailty and the brevity of life under God's wrath against sin. Wisdom is produced by honest reckoning with mortality in light of God's eternity.

text: Do they not err that devise evil? but mercy and truth shall be to them that devise good.
digest: {firstname}, those who devise evil erring, while mercy and truth belong to those who devise good, reflects wisdom's principle that outcomes are tied to the intentions behind actions. God's own character, mercy and truth, is what those who plan good ultimately reflect and receive.

text: Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
digest: {firstname}, redeeming the time "because the days are evil" comes within Paul's instruction to walk as wise, not as fools, filled with the Spirit rather than with wine. Wise use of time is set here as a mark of Spirit-filled living amid a fallen age.

text: Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.
digest: {firstname}, trusting God at all times and pouring out one's heart before Him, with God described as "a refuge for us," continues this psalm's meditation on God alone as rock and salvation. Honest, unguarded prayer before God, not composed self-presentation, is what this verse invites.

text: To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.
digest: {firstname}, doing justice and judgment being more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice reflects a recurring prophetic and wisdom theme that ritual observance without righteous action fails to please God. Right conduct toward others matters to God even more than religious ceremony performed without it.

text: Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain.
digest: {firstname}, Paul's comparison of the Christian life to a race in which only one receives the prize, urging believers to run so as to obtain it, precedes his own description of disciplining his body like an athlete. This is not competition against fellow believers but wholehearted pursuit of the imperishable crown Christ offers.

text: The meek will he guide in judgment: and the meek will he teach his way.
digest: {firstname}, the meek being guided in judgment and taught God's way continues this acrostic psalm's theme of humble dependence on the Lord's instruction. Teachable humility, this psalm shows, is what actually opens a person to being rightly led by God.

text: He that tilleth his land shall be satisfied with bread: but he that followeth vain persons is void of understanding.
digest: {firstname}, the one who tills his land being satisfied with bread, while pursuit of vain things shows lack of understanding, reflects wisdom's value of attentive, faithful labor over distraction by empty pursuits. Diligence toward one's actual responsibilities is commended over chasing lesser things.

text: And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge;
digest: {firstname}, adding diligence and virtue to faith opens Peter's extended list of qualities believers are to build upon their faith, culminating in the assurance that these will keep one from being unfruitful. Faith, in Peter's teaching, is meant to actively grow into a fuller Christian character, not remain static.

text: Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them.
digest: {firstname}, blessing on the one whose strength is in God, "in whose heart are the ways of them," pictures pilgrims journeying to Zion, strengthened along the way, within this psalm celebrating the courts of the Lord. Life is pictured here as a pilgrimage sustained by God's strength toward His presence, the ultimate destination.

text: Let not thine heart envy sinners: but be thou in the fear of the LORD all the day long.
digest: {firstname}, the heart instructed not to envy sinners but to remain in the fear of the Lord continually addresses the wisdom tradition's concern that apparent prosperity of the wicked might tempt covenant faithfulness. Sustained reverence for God, not comparison to sinners' apparent gain, is the proper response commended here.

text: But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment.
digest: {firstname}, the warning that people will give account for every idle word on the day of judgment comes within Jesus' teaching on the tree known by its fruit, following the Pharisees' slanderous accusation against Him. Careless speech, this passage teaches, reveals the heart's true condition and will be judged accordingly.

text: Behold, the eye of the LORD is upon them that fear him, upon them that hope in his mercy;
digest: {firstname}, the Lord's eye upon those who fear Him and hope in His mercy continues this psalm's celebration of God's sovereign word over creation and the futility of relying on military might. God's attentive favor rests specifically on those who trust Him, not on those who trust their own strength.

text: A man hath joy by the answer of his mouth: and a word spoken in due season, how good is it!
digest: {firstname}, joy in the answer of one's own mouth, and a word spoken in due season called good, reflects wisdom's attention to how timing shapes the value of even a true and well-formed word. Fitting timing is part of what makes speech genuinely good, not merely accurate.

text: Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
digest: {firstname}, boldly approaching the throne of grace for mercy and help comes immediately after the description of Christ as great high priest who sympathizes with human weakness, having been tempted in every way yet without sin. This boldness is possible only because of Christ's priestly work, not because of confidence in oneself.

text: As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
digest: {firstname}, the soul's longing for God compared to a deer panting after water brooks opens a psalm of deep spiritual thirst, written by one apparently exiled from the temple's worship. This longing is presented as urgent and essential, like physical thirst, not optional devotion.

text: There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, but it tendeth to poverty.
digest: {firstname}, one who scatters generously still increasing, while withholding more than is meet leads to poverty, reflects wisdom's counterintuitive principle that generosity, not hoarding, is the path to true increase. This anticipates the fuller New Testament teaching on giving and receiving.

text: As ye have therefore received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk ye in him:
digest: {firstname}, walking in Christ Jesus the Lord in the same manner He was received, by faith, comes within Paul's warning against being led astray by philosophy and empty deceit. Continuing in the faith mirrors the manner of its beginning: by grace through faith, not human tradition.

text: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
digest: {firstname}, praise for being "fearfully and wonderfully made" comes within this psalm's extended meditation on God's intimate knowledge of the psalmist from conception onward. Being known this completely by the Creator is the ground for praise, not primarily for self-esteem.

text: Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
digest: {firstname}, fire going out without wood, and strife ceasing without a talebearer, reflects wisdom's identification of gossip as the specific fuel that sustains conflict. Removing the source of contentious speech is what wisdom prescribes for ending strife.

text: There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.
digest: {firstname}, perfect love casting out fear, because fear involves torment, comes within John's extended teaching that God is love and that love is perfected in believers as they abide in Him. Mature love, rooted in God's own perfect love demonstrated through Christ, displaces the torment of fear rather than merely coexisting with it.

text: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him.
digest: {firstname}, God's pity toward those who fear Him, compared to a father's pity for his children, continues this psalm's extended description of the Lord's mercy, forgiveness, and covenant love. This comparison grounds divine compassion in the most intimate human relationship, yet infinitely surpassing it.

text: Ponder the path of thy feet, and let all thy ways be established.
digest: {firstname}, pondering the path of one's feet so that all ways may be established continues this chapter's instruction to guard the heart and remove crooked speech. Deliberate reflection before action, not impulsive movement, is what establishes a person's ways securely.

text: He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
digest: {firstname}, God covering with His feathers, under whose wings one may trust, with His truth as shield and buckler, continues this psalm's extended description of divine protection for the one who dwells in His secret place. The imagery here is maternal and near, close covering rather than distant oversight.

text: Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.
digest: {firstname}, believers called "the light of the world," a city on a hill that cannot be hidden, follows the Beatitudes and precedes Jesus' teaching that good works should be seen so that the Father is glorified. Visibility of righteous conduct is presented as the natural, unavoidable nature of light, not something believers must manufacture.

text: When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.
digest: {firstname}, when a person's ways please the Lord, He makes even enemies to be at peace, reflecting the wisdom tradition's confidence that right relationship with God can reshape human relationships. Reconciliation with others is tied here, surprisingly, to right standing before God first.

text: The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?
digest: {firstname}, the Lord being on the psalmist's side, so that he will not fear what man can do, continues this psalm celebrating God's steadfast love, later applied by the New Testament to Christ as the rejected stone become the cornerstone. Confidence here rests entirely on whose side one stands, secured ultimately in the God who vindicates the righteous.

text: Now he that planteth and he that watereth are one: and every man shall receive his own reward according to his own labour.
digest: {firstname}, the one who plants and the one who waters being one, each rewarded according to his own labor, comes within Paul's rebuke of factions dividing over which apostle they follow. Different roles within the same gospel work are valued individually by God, not ranked competitively against one another.

text: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.
digest: {firstname}, hope deferred making the heart sick, but desire fulfilled as a tree of life, reflects wisdom literature's honest acknowledgment of the real pain that comes with prolonged, unmet longing. Scripture takes seriously the ache of delayed hope without dismissing its legitimacy.

text: But thou, O LORD, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord as shield, glory, and the lifter of the head, was written, according to its superscription, while David fled from his son Absalom. Being lifted here pictures reversal of deep humiliation and discouragement, not merely defense against attack.

text: We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
digest: {firstname}, the strong bearing the weaknesses of the weak, not merely pleasing themselves, comes within Paul's extended instruction on unity between Jewish and Gentile believers regarding disputable matters. Strength in the faith carries an obligation toward weaker believers, following the pattern of Christ described just after, who did not please Himself.

text: It is an honour for a man to cease from strife: but every fool will be meddling.
digest: {firstname}, honor belonging to the one who ceases from strife, while every fool is quick to quarrel, reframes walking away from unnecessary conflict as dignity rather than weakness. Wisdom values peace pursued deliberately over contention entered carelessly.

text: What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee.
digest: {firstname}, the declaration "what time I am afraid, I will trust in thee" was written, according to its superscription, when the Philistines seized David in Gath. Trust exercised precisely amid genuine fear, not the absence of fear, is what this psalm models.

text: But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.
digest: {firstname}, "with man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" answers the disciples' astonished question about who then can be saved, following Jesus' teaching on the difficulty of the rich entering the kingdom. Salvation itself, this passage teaches, exceeds human capacity and rests entirely on God's power.

text: He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends.
digest: {firstname}, covering a transgression seeking love, while repeating a matter separates close friends, identifies the corrosive effect of dwelling on old offenses within relationships. Love that covers, rather than rehearses, wrongs preserves what repetition of grievance destroys.

text: The LORD will give strength unto his people; the LORD will bless his people with peace.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord giving strength to His people and blessing them with peace closes a psalm depicting God's voice in the storm, enthroned as King over the flood. The same God whose voice commands the mighty storm gives strength and peace to His own people.

text: For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
digest: {firstname}, the outward man perishing while the inward man is renewed daily comes within Paul's discussion of present affliction producing "a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory." Decline and renewal happen simultaneously in the believer's experience, sustained by looking to unseen, eternal things.

text: Every wise woman buildeth her house: but the foolish plucketh it down with her hands.
digest: {firstname}, the wise woman building her house while the foolish tears it down with her own hands attributes real, tangible consequence to daily choices made within the household. Wisdom or folly in ordinary domestic life carries lasting weight in this proverb's assessment.

text: Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies.
digest: {firstname}, doing valiantly through God, who will tread down enemies, closes a psalm combining earlier praise with a plea for help, crediting all victory to God's power, not human strength. Valor here is entirely derivative, accomplished through God working on His people's behalf.

text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
digest: {firstname}, being swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath comes within James' instruction on receiving the implanted word with meekness, following his teaching that human anger does not produce God's righteousness. The order given here, listening first, is essential to the righteous life James describes throughout his letter.

text: The merciful man doeth good to his own soul: but he that is cruel troubleth his own flesh.
digest: {firstname}, the merciful man doing good to his own soul, the cruel troubling his own flesh, reflects wisdom's principle that how one treats others returns to affect oneself. Mercy shown to others is never merely outward-facing; it shapes the giver as well.

text: For thou art my rock and my fortress; therefore for thy name's sake lead me, and guide me.
digest: {firstname}, God as rock and fortress, asked to lead and guide "for thy name's sake," continues this psalm of trust amid persecution, later quoted by Jesus from the cross. Guidance sought here is tied to the honoring of God's own name, not merely personal benefit.

text: Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
digest: {firstname}, taking Christ's yoke and learning from Him, because He is meek and lowly in heart, follows His invitation to the weary and burdened and precedes His promise that His yoke is easy and burden light. Rest for the soul is found specifically in submission to and instruction from Christ's own humble character.

text: He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.
digest: {firstname}, the bountiful eye being blessed because it gives bread to the poor reflects wisdom's description of generosity almost as a way of seeing, an eye inclined toward others' need. This generous disposition, not mere occasional charity, is what this proverb commends and blesses.

text: Thou crownest the year with thy goodness; and thy paths drop fatness.
digest: {firstname}, God crowning the year with goodness, with paths dropping fatness, closes a psalm celebrating God's provision through rain and harvest as evidence of His faithful care over creation. Abundance is pictured here as flowing wherever God's blessing moves across the created order.

text: Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:
digest: {firstname}, humbling oneself under God's mighty hand so that He may exalt "in due time" comes within Peter's instruction to cast all anxiety upon God, who cares for His people, amid warnings about the adversary. Exaltation's timing is left entirely to God's sovereign wisdom, following the pattern of humility He honors.

text: A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit.
digest: {firstname}, a wholesome tongue as a tree of life, contrasted with perverseness that breaks the spirit, reflects wisdom's consistent teaching that speech carries life-giving or damaging power, with little neutral ground between. The tongue's effect here is treated as genuinely consequential, not incidental.

text: And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.
digest: {firstname}, God putting a new song of praise in the mouth, so that many will see and trust in the Lord, continues this psalm of deliverance from the pit and miry clay described earlier. Personal testimony of God's deliverance is shown here to have a public, evangelistic effect on others.

text: For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,
digest: {firstname}, Paul's exhaustive list, death, life, angels, powers, present, future, nothing able to separate believers from God's love in Christ Jesus, closes this triumphant chapter following the doctrine of predestination and God's unstoppable purpose for the elect. This assurance rests on the completed, unbreakable work of Christ, not on the believer's own consistency.

text: He that getteth wisdom loveth his own soul: he that keepeth understanding shall find good.
digest: {firstname}, the one who gets wisdom loving his own soul, keeping understanding to find good, presents pursuit of wisdom as an act of genuine self-love rightly ordered, not opposed to self-interest but fulfilling it truly. Wisdom and true flourishing are inseparably connected in this proverb.

text: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.
digest: {firstname}, goodness and mercy following the psalmist all his days, dwelling in the Lord's house forever, closes this shepherd psalm that began with confession of the Lord's sufficient provision. This is covenant assurance of God's pursuing faithfulness through life and into eternity, not merely a hope for a trouble-free existence.

text: Be not ye therefore like unto them: for your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him.
digest: {firstname}, the Father already knowing what is needed before it is asked comes immediately before Jesus teaches the Lord's Prayer as the pattern for right petition. Prayer is not meant to inform an unknowing God but to align the heart with the Father who already knows and provides.

text: A man shall be satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth: and the recompence of a man's hands shall be rendered unto him.
digest: {firstname}, satisfaction with good coming by the fruit of one's mouth, and the recompense of one's hands returning to him, reflects wisdom's principle that both speech and labor yield a kind of harvest to the one who produces them. Words and works are both credited with real, returning consequence.

text: Order my steps in thy word: and let not any iniquity have dominion over me.
digest: {firstname}, the request that steps be ordered in God's word, with no iniquity having dominion, continues this extended psalm's dependence on Scripture for both guidance and deliverance from sin's rule. Freedom from sin's dominion is sought here through God's word, not assumed as automatic.

text: Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby.
digest: {firstname}, chastening seeming grievous rather than joyous at the time, yet later yielding "the peaceable fruit of righteousness" to those trained by it, comes within the author's extended comparison of God's discipline to a father's loving correction. This honest acknowledgment of discipline's pain does not diminish its ultimately sanctifying purpose.

text: Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established:
digest: {firstname}, a house built through wisdom and established by understanding continues this chapter's instruction contrasting wise strength with the folly of laziness. The durability of any household or endeavor is credited here to the wisdom underlying its construction, not mere effort.

text: Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand.
digest: {firstname}, though a good man falls, he shall not be utterly cast down, for the Lord upholds him with His hand, continues this psalm's sustained contrast between the righteous and the wicked's respective destinies. Falling is acknowledged as real even for the righteous, but never final, because of God's sustaining grip.

text: But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.
digest: {firstname}, the Spirit's manifestation given to each person "to profit withal," meaning for the common good, opens Paul's extended teaching on spiritual gifts and the body of Christ. Every gift is distributed by the Spirit with the whole church's benefit in view, never for private advantage alone.

text: Ointment and perfume rejoice the heart: so doth the sweetness of a man's friend by hearty counsel.
digest: {firstname}, ointment and perfume rejoicing the heart, matched by the sweetness of a friend's hearty counsel, reflects wisdom's high value placed on honest, caring advice from a genuine friend. Godly counsel offered in friendship is compared here to something genuinely delightful, not merely useful.

text: God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early.
digest: {firstname}, God in the midst of her, so she shall not be moved, helping "right early," continues this psalm's imagery of God's city standing secure amid cosmic upheaval described earlier. Help here comes from God's presence within the situation itself, not from a distant intervention.

text: Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you:
digest: {firstname}, ask, seek, knock, each promised its corresponding answer, comes within the Sermon on the Mount just before Jesus compares the Father's goodness to that of an earthly father who gives good gifts to his children. Persistent, ongoing prayer is commended here, grounded in confidence in the Father's good character.

text: The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord's blessing making rich, adding no sorrow with it, distinguishes blessing that flows from God from gain acquired by other, more troubled means described elsewhere in this chapter. True enrichment from God is marked by the absence of the sorrow that accompanies ill-gotten or anxiously grasped wealth.

text: The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger: but they that seek the LORD shall not want any good thing.
digest: {firstname}, young lions lacking and suffering hunger, while those who seek the Lord lack no good thing, continues this psalm's testimony following David's deliverance before Abimelech. Even creatures known for strength can go hungry, while those who seek God are promised a more reliable sufficiency than strength alone provides.

text: Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us,
digest: {firstname}, God able to do "exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us" closes Paul's prayer for the Ephesians' strengthening, rooted in the same power that raised Christ from the dead, described earlier in the letter. This doxology grounds limitless divine capability in the very power already at work within believers.

text: A just weight and balance are the LORD'S: all the weights of the bag are his work.
digest: {firstname}, a just weight and balance belonging to the Lord, with all the weights in the bag being His work, ties fairness in ordinary commercial dealings directly to God's own character and ownership. Honest dealing reflects the moral order God has built into the world, not merely social convention.

text: Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.
digest: {firstname}, David's request to restore the joy of salvation and be upheld by a willing spirit continues his psalm of repentance after his sin with Bathsheba, following his plea for a clean heart. Joy lost through sin is something David asks to have restored by God, not something he attempts to manufacture through self-effort.

text: Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer;
digest: {firstname}, rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation, continuing steadfastly in prayer, comes within Paul's list of marks of genuine, Spirit-transformed love described throughout this chapter. These three postures are meant to be held together continuously, not selected individually depending on circumstance.

text: When thou liest down, thou shalt not be afraid: yea, thou shalt lie down, and thy sleep shall be sweet.
digest: {firstname}, lying down without fear, with sweet sleep, follows this chapter's earlier instruction to keep sound wisdom and discretion, which are described as life to the soul. Untroubled rest here is the fruit of the trust and wisdom commended throughout this passage, not an isolated promise.

text: For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south.
digest: {firstname}, promotion coming from neither east, west, nor south, implying it comes from God alone as judge, continues this psalm's declaration that God alone lifts up and puts down. Advancement in this world is credited here entirely to God's sovereign judgment, not human positioning or effort.

text: But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;
digest: {firstname}, loving enemies, blessing those who curse, and praying for those who mistreat you, comes within Jesus' teaching that fulfills and exceeds the Old Testament law's demand, calling disciples to be perfect as their heavenly Father is perfect. This command reflects the Father's own character, who sends rain on the just and unjust alike, as the following verse states.

text: The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
digest: {firstname}, the horse prepared for battle, yet safety belonging to the Lord, reflects wisdom's consistent teaching that human preparation, while necessary, is never ultimately sufficient apart from God's sovereign deliverance. Diligent effort and total dependence on God are held together, not opposed, in this proverb.

text: The LORD upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that be bowed down.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord upholding all who fall and raising up all who are bowed down continues this psalm's sweeping celebration of God's universal goodness and compassion over all His works. This is described as God's general, ongoing pattern of care, not a rare exception to His usual dealings.

text: But godliness with contentment is great gain.
digest: {firstname}, godliness with contentment as "great gain" comes within Paul's warning against false teachers who suppose godliness is a means of financial gain. True gain, Paul redefines here, is the settled contentment that accompanies genuine faith, not material accumulation.

text: In the fear of the LORD is strong confidence: and his children shall have a place of refuge.
digest: {firstname}, strong confidence in the fear of the Lord, with His children finding a place of refuge, reflects wisdom's consistent grounding of confidence in reverence for God rather than self-assurance. This refuge extends specifically to those within covenant relationship with Him, described here as His children.

text: I had fainted, unless I had believed to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living.
digest: {firstname}, the psalmist's confession that he would have fainted unless believing he would see the Lord's goodness "in the land of the living" comes near the end of a psalm moving from confident trust to earnest plea amid enemies. Belief in God's goodness sustained him precisely through a moment that otherwise felt unbearable.

text: The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus contrasting the thief who comes to steal, kill, and destroy with His own purpose, that His sheep might have life abundantly, comes within His extended teaching identifying Himself as the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. Abundant life is secured specifically through the good shepherd's sacrificial death, described later in the same discourse.

text: A man's gift maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men.
digest: {firstname}, a person's gift making room for them, bringing them before great men, reflects wisdom's observation that genuine, well-used ability tends to open doors on its own merit. This proverb notices a general pattern of providence working through developed gifts.

text: I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations.
digest: {firstname}, singing of the Lord's mercies forever, making His faithfulness known to all generations, opens a psalm that extensively recounts God's covenant with David before lamenting its apparent failure. Even amid confusion over unfulfilled promise, this psalm begins by anchoring itself in God's proven, covenantal faithfulness.

text: Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
digest: {firstname}, sent out as sheep among wolves, to be wise as serpents and harmless as doves, comes within Jesus' commissioning of the twelve, warning them of coming persecution for His name's sake. This pairing of shrewdness and gentleness equips disciples to navigate real hostility without compromising integrity.

text: The light of the eyes rejoiceth the heart: and a good report maketh the bones fat.
digest: {firstname}, the light of the eyes rejoicing the heart, and good news making the bones healthy, reflects wisdom's consistent connection between good tidings, cheerful countenance, and genuine physical wellbeing. Good news is credited here with restorative power reaching the whole person.

text: Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art the God of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day.
digest: {firstname}, being led in God's truth and taught, because He is "the God of my salvation," on whom the psalmist waits all day, continues this acrostic psalm's theme of humble, continuous dependence on God's instruction. Waiting here is described as filling the entire day, a sustained posture rather than a brief pause.

text: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
digest: {firstname}, all Scripture given by inspiration of God, profitable for doctrine, reproof, correction, and instruction in righteousness, comes just before Paul states its purpose: that the man of God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work. Scripture's inspiration and sufficiency for both teaching and correcting are affirmed together here.

text: The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the LORD trieth the hearts.
digest: {firstname}, the fining pot for silver, the furnace for gold, but the Lord testing hearts, applies refining imagery specifically to the inner person, suggesting purpose behind divine testing. God's testing of the heart is presented here as purifying, not merely punitive.

text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.
digest: {firstname}, going in the strength of the Lord, making mention of His righteousness alone, continues this psalm of an aging believer pleading for continued help, deliberately setting aside every other possible source of confidence. Sole reliance on God's righteousness, not accumulated personal merit, is the psalmist's explicit ground for confidence.

text: But let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another.
digest: {firstname}, examining one's own work so as to have rejoicing in oneself alone, not in comparison to another, comes within Paul's instruction on gently restoring a fallen brother while watching one's own susceptibility to temptation. Self-examination replaces comparison as the appropriate basis for any confidence in this passage.

text: Counsel in the heart of man is like deep water; but a man of understanding will draw it out.
digest: {firstname}, counsel in the heart compared to deep water, drawn out by a person of understanding, reflects wisdom's recognition that real insight often requires patient effort to access, both in oneself and in others. Understanding here is credited with the ability to draw out what otherwise remains hidden.

text: Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah.
digest: {firstname}, God as hiding place, preserving from trouble and surrounding with songs of deliverance, comes within this psalm of forgiveness following David's confession of sin described in its opening verses. Even in hiding from trouble, there is singing here, the fruit of forgiveness already received.

text: But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
digest: {firstname}, good ground representing the one who hears the word and understands it, bearing fruit at varying measure, closes Jesus' parable of the sower with His explanation of the different soils. Understanding, not merely hearing, is what this parable ties directly to genuine, lasting fruitfulness.

text: The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
digest: {firstname}, the wicked fleeing when no one pursues, while the righteous are bold as a lion, reflects wisdom's contrast between the unsettled conscience of guilt and the steady confidence a clear conscience allows. Boldness here flows from righteousness, not from circumstance being free of threat.

text: For the LORD is good; his mercy is everlasting; and his truth endureth to all generations.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord's goodness, everlasting mercy, and enduring truth "to all generations" closes this psalm of thanksgiving calling all lands to serve the Lord with gladness. Three enduring qualities of God's character are named here as the very basis for joyful worship.

text: Let all things be done decently and in order.
digest: {firstname}, all things done "decently and in order" closes Paul's extended instructions on orderly worship, addressing the misuse of spiritual gifts within the Corinthian church. Thoughtful order in worship, Paul teaches, reflects God's own character as a God of peace, not confusion, stated earlier in the passage.

text: The rich ruleth over the poor, and the borrower is servant to the lender.
digest: {firstname}, the rich ruling over the poor, and the borrower becoming servant to the lender, names honestly the real power dynamic that debt creates between parties. This proverb offers sober wisdom about financial dependency worth heeding before entering into it.

text: Our soul waiteth for the LORD: he is our help and our shield.
digest: {firstname}, the soul waiting for the Lord, described as help and shield, closes this psalm celebrating God's sovereign word over creation and His frustration of nations' plans described earlier. Waiting here is paired with confident expectation, grounded in who is being waited upon, not passive uncertainty.

text: Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
digest: {firstname}, holding fast the confession of faith without wavering, "for he is faithful that promised," comes within the author's call to draw near to God with full assurance, having been cleansed through Christ's blood. The steadiness required of believers rests entirely on the proven steadiness of the God who made the promise.

text: A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.
digest: {firstname}, a good man leaving an inheritance to his children's children, while the sinner's wealth is stored up for the just, reflects wisdom's long view of how possessions eventually settle according to God's moral ordering of history. This proverb takes the generational and ultimate outworking of righteousness and wickedness seriously.

text: For thou, LORD, wilt bless the righteous; with favour wilt thou compass him as with a shield.
digest: {firstname}, the Lord blessing the righteous, surrounding them with favor "as with a shield," closes a morning prayer contrasting the fate of the wicked with God's covenant care for those who trust Him. This surrounding favor is comprehensive protection, not partial or occasional.

text: But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
digest: {firstname}, wisdom from above described as first pure, then peaceable, gentle, willing to yield, full of mercy and good fruits, contrasts sharply with the earthly, sensual, demonic wisdom James describes just before. Heavenly wisdom is defined here by its moral character, not merely its cleverness or persuasiveness.

text: Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish.
digest: {firstname}, loving instruction as loving knowledge, while hating correction is called "brutish," reflects wisdom's consistent measure of true wisdom by one's willingness to receive correction. Response to correction functions here as a genuine test of whether a person actually values wisdom.

text: Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me: thou shalt stretch forth thine hand against the wrath of mine enemies, and thy right hand shall save me.
digest: {firstname}, God reviving the psalmist in the midst of trouble, stretching out His hand against the wrath of enemies, continues this psalm of thanksgiving anticipating all earth's kings praising God's word. Revival happens here in the middle of trouble, not merely after deliverance from it.

text: Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.
digest: {firstname}, Christ's promise to be with His disciples always, "even unto the end of the world," closes the Great Commission, given immediately after Jesus declares all authority in heaven and earth has been given to Him. His abiding presence is promised specifically alongside the church's ongoing task of making disciples, secured by His universal authority.

text: The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that winneth souls is wise.
digest: {firstname}, the fruit of the righteous as a tree of life, and the one who wins souls being wise, ties a righteous life's fruit directly to bringing others toward life as well. This proverb connects personal righteousness with fruitful influence upon others, not mere private virtue.

text: Because thou hast been my help, therefore in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice.
digest: {firstname}, rejoicing in the shadow of God's wings because He has been "my help" continues this psalm of earnest seeking, likely written while David was in the wilderness of Judah. Rejoicing here follows remembered help already received, not merely present circumstances alone.

text: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
digest: {firstname}, faith coming by hearing, and hearing by the word of God, comes within Paul's argument for the necessity of gospel proclamation so that people might call upon the Lord and be saved. Faith is described here as generated through continued exposure to the proclaimed word of Christ, not a fixed inner resource.

text: By mercy and truth iniquity is purged: and by the fear of the LORD men depart from evil.
digest: {firstname}, iniquity purged by mercy and truth, and departure from evil through the fear of the Lord, describes these qualities working together to actually redirect a person's moral trajectory. Mercy and truth, reflecting God's own character, are credited here with genuine transforming power.

text: In the day of my trouble I will call upon thee: for thou wilt answer me.
digest: {firstname}, calling upon God in the day of trouble because He will answer, continues David's prayer appealing to God's mercy, goodness, and readiness to forgive described throughout this psalm. Confidence to call on God rests on an already-formed expectation, grounded in His revealed character, that He does answer.

text: And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us:
digest: {firstname}, the confidence that God hears prayers made "according to his will" comes within John's closing assurances to believers regarding eternal life and answered prayer. Confidence in prayer is tied specifically to alignment with God's revealed will, not certainty about receiving whatever is requested.

text: But the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
digest: {firstname}, the path of the just like the shining light, growing brighter unto the perfect day, contrasts with the way of the wicked, described as darkness in the following verse. Growth in righteousness is pictured here as gradual and progressive, moving toward the fullness of glory yet to come.

text: It is a good thing to give thanks unto the LORD, and to sing praises unto thy name, O most High:
digest: {firstname}, the goodness of giving thanks and singing praises to God's name opens a psalm for the Sabbath day, celebrating God's works and His enduring exaltation over all. Thanksgiving and praise are affirmed here simply as good in themselves, fitting responses to who God is.

text: But when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them, because they fainted, and were scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd.
digest: {firstname}, Jesus moved with compassion at the sight of crowds "scattered abroad, as sheep having no shepherd," precedes His instruction to the disciples to pray for laborers for the plentiful harvest. His compassion responds to the crowd's spiritual condition itself, not merely to a request they had made.

text: Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
digest: {firstname}, strength and honor as her clothing, able to rejoice in time to come, describes the virtuous woman celebrated throughout this closing chapter of Proverbs. Character described here, wisdom, diligence, and the fear of the Lord noted in the following verses, is what grounds genuine confidence about the future.

text: Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.
digest: {firstname}, "let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD" closes the entire Psalter, following an extended call to praise God with every instrument available. Praise belonging to everything that has breath reflects the fitting, universal response owed to God by all His creation.
